units.idea: A measurement needs both a number and a unit.
units.explanation: A unit is the amount we use to measure, such as a metre. The number tells us how many of those units fit. Changing the unit changes the number, but not the object.

example.title: The same shelf
steps: A shelf is 1.8 metres long.
Each metre contains 100 centimetres, so 1.8 × 100 = 180 centimetres.
The shelf stays the same length.

terms.definition: An agreed amount used for measuring.

scale.idea: Powers of ten are a short way to write very large or small numbers.
scale.explanation: The raised number tells us how many tens to multiply. A negative raised number means divide 1 by those tens; it does not make the answer negative.

example.title: A thin coating
steps: A coating is 6 × 10⁻⁴ metres thick.
Six of these make 0.0006 metres.

terms.definition: A number made by multiplying tens, or by dividing 1 by that product.

relationships.idea: An equation shows how quantities are connected.
relationships.explanation: A quantity is something we can measure. At a steady speed, an object travels the same distance each second. Multiplying that speed by the time gives the distance.

example.title: A moving belt
steps: A belt moves 0.4 metres each second for 5 seconds.
It travels 0.4 × 5 = 2 metres.

terms.definition: Something we can measure, such as distance or time.

vectors.idea: A vector tells us both how much and which way.
vectors.explanation: We draw a vector as an arrow. A displacement arrow points straight from the start to the finish. Its length can be shorter than the path travelled.

example.title: A rover turns a corner
steps: A rover drives 6 metres east and then 8 metres north.
These directions make a right angle, so the straight arrow has length √(6² + 8²) = 10 metres.
That arrow describes where the rover finishes relative to its start.

terms.definition: A quantity with both size and direction.
The change from starting position to finishing position.
Positive square root: the nonnegative number whose square gives the value inside.

graphs.idea: A position–time graph shows where an object is at each time.
graphs.explanation: Time runs along the bottom and position runs up the side. To find average velocity, divide the position change by the time taken. Velocity includes direction.

example.title: Reading two points
steps: At 1 second, the object is at 2 metres; at 4 seconds, it is at 8 metres.
Its position changes by 6 metres in 3 seconds.
Its average velocity is +2 metres per second.

terms.definition: Where something is compared with a chosen zero point.
Position change divided by elapsed time, including direction.

accumulation.idea: Add the change in each part of a trip to find the overall change.
accumulation.explanation: Choose one direction as positive. Motion the other way counts as negative. Adding these signed changes tells you where the trip ends compared with where it began.

example.title: A trip to the right and back
steps: Moving right at 2 metres per second for 3 seconds adds +6 metres.
Moving left at 1 metre per second for 2 seconds adds −2 metres.
The overall change is +4 metres: the finish is 4 metres right of the start.

uncertainty.idea: A measurement is an estimate with a stated amount of uncertainty.
uncertainty.explanation: Uncertainty describes how much doubt remains in a measurement. Compare it with the size of the estimate to see how large that doubt is in proportion. The method used to find the uncertainty still matters.

example.title: Measuring a length
steps: A length estimate is 40 centimetres, with stated uncertainty of 1 centimetre.
Divide 1 by 40 to get 0.025, or 2.5%.
This comparison does not, by itself, say how likely any particular length is.

terms.definition: A stated measure of doubt about a measurement.
Uncertainty divided by the size of the estimate.

models.idea: A model is a simplified description used to answer a question.
models.explanation: We choose which details matter, then use the model to predict a result. Compare that prediction with measurements. A disagreement is a reason to check the model and measurements.

example.title: Predicting a trolley's motion
steps: Suppose a trolley keeps moving forward at 0.6 metres per second.
In 5 seconds, the model predicts 0.6 × 5 = 3 metres forward.
Compare that prediction with how far the trolley actually moves.

terms.definition: A simplified description used to answer a question.
A result expected if the model's conditions hold.
